newsitem.title: UK: UK August PMI index 51.8, highest for a year.
newsitem.headline: UK August PMI index 51.8, highest for a year.

text.p: The UK Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) rose to a seasonally adjusted 51.8 percent in August, its highest level for a year, from an upwardly revised 51.0 percent in July, the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said on Monday.
"Both output and new order levels expanded more rapidly than at any time since the spring of 1995," it said in its August Report on Business.

"This suggests that the slowdown in manufacturing activity, which began in late 1994, probably bottomed out in May. Since then, rising consumers' expenditure has been the main driving force behind steadily accelerating growth in the manufacturing sector."

The survey suggested mounting demand for consumer goods had begun to feed down the supply chain, with producers of intermediate goods seeing warehouse stocks of unsold goods falling very sharply for the third month in a row.
"In order to restock warehouses and meet higher demand, output of intermediate goods rose sharply," the CIPS said.
The prices index rose to 41.5 in August from 38.5 in July but remained at a very low level by the survey's historical standards.
"Just under a quarter of all companies saw the average price paid for their purchases fall," the report said.
The employment index edged up to 50.1 from 49.7 in July, suggesting a flat picture.
"The incidence of redundancies fell compared with July but take-up of permanent staff was generally reported to have remained subdued by continued uncertainty about future business prospects."
Following is a table of seasonally adjusted PMI indices (previously reported July figures in brackets):
AUGUST JULY (pvs)
Purchasing Managers Index 51.8 51.0 (50.9)
Quantity of Purchases 50.0 47.7 (47.3)
Suppliers delivery times 50.3 52.2 (52.6)
Stocks of Purchases 47.1 45.1 (45.0)
Stocks of Finished Goods 45.1 44.8 (44.9)
Employment 50.1 49.7 (49.7)
NOTE: The PMI is based on a weighted average of seasonally adjusted measures of output, new orders, suppliers' delivery times, stocks of items purchased and employment.

The measures are turned into indices which vary around 50 percent, a level which indicates no change on the previous month. An index reading below 50 percent indicates a decline compared with the previous month, above 50 percent an increase.
